title: When does conformal calibration need censoring weights?Cause-of-failure prediction sets under competing risks

paper.title:
When does conformal calibration need censoring weights? Cause-of-failure
prediction sets under competing risks
paper.abstract:
Abstract Split conformal prediction sets for competing-risks labels at a fixed horizon
require calibration labels that right censoring can leave unobserved.
Complete-case calibration guarantees coverage for the label-complete
subpopulation, but its population coverage can deviate in either direction, even
at the true class probabilities. We study how selection changes the score
distribution near the population quantile. At the true score in our main
simulation family, with independent draws, complete-case calibration covers
0.8723 at a nominal 0.900 when 22% of subjects are event-free at the horizon. In
4 of 48 further designs using per-draw normalisation, estimating cause incidences
as one minus the exponential of the negative of the cause-specific Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazards, with the
event-free probability as the clipped and renormalised remainder, puts
complete-case coverage at least four standard errors below nominal. In these
designs, weights from a correctly specified censoring model keep coverage near
nominal. Extending the argument of Yi et al. (2025) to a cause label, we
establish a finite-sample coverage lower bound with an explicit penalty for
censoring-model error. Misspecifying the censoring model can also lead to
under-coverage.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: For a competing-risks model, a natural prediction at a fixed horizon is a set of causes, possibly including event-free status, that contains the realised label at the horizon for at least 1 − α 1-\alpha of subjects. Split conformal prediction gives such a set from any fitted model when the calibration labels are observed. Under right censoring they are not, since a subject who leaves follow-up before the horizon without an event has no label. Complete-case calibration keeps the subjects whose label is determined and drops the rest. It selects on the outcome, because a subject who fails early is more likely to have been followed long enough than one who survives past the horizon, and the exchangeability that conformal prediction relies on is lost. Boström et al. (2019) use this procedure for a binary event-by-horizon label and state its guarantee for the subjects not censored before the horizon. Boström et al. (2023) keep the censored subjects, with a Kaplan–Meier estimate within each Mondrian category, to give a predictive distribution for the event time. Reports on the population disagree. Dang et al. (2026) find complete-case conformal under-covering, attribute it to the censoring rate and recommend a switch above 40%. Farina et al. (2026) find their complete-case comparator over-covering in every setting they run, but their target is a lower prediction bound on the event time, for which selection toward short observed times is conservative by construction. Neither account applies to a label at a horizon. We characterise when complete-case calibration is safe for a cause-of-failure label and when weighting the calibration sample by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored repairs it. The paper makes three contributions. 1. The complete-case error can take either sign, even at the true score. Complete-case calibration takes its threshold from the score distribution of the selected subjects, and we study how this selection changes coverage over the population. At fixed covariates, subjects event-free at the horizon have the lowest selection probability, so the event-free share, error in the fitted event-free probability and the dependence of censoring on the covariates all shift the selected score distribution relative to the population’s. The direction of the mean score shift indicates the sign of the error but does not determine it (Appendix F ). In our main simulation family at the true score, the unweighted procedure over-covers at an event-free share of 0.544 0.544 and under-covers at 0.224 0.224 , where it covers 0.8723 0.8723 at a nominal 0.900 0.900 over 200 200 replications with independent draws (Section 4.1 ). In a two-region law where most subjects are event-free, the true score still under-covers (Section 4.3 ). A fit that understates the event-free probability lowers coverage, censoring amplifies both effects, and the observed crossing point moves with the censoring rate, so no threshold on the censoring rate locates the failure. Estimating each cause’s incidence as one minus a cause-specific survival curve, with the event-free probability as the remainder, puts the unweighted procedure at least four standard errors below nominal in 4 of 48 designs (Section 4.2 ). 2. Censoring weights give a coverage guarantee for any score when the censoring model is correct. In the studied designs with covariate-free censoring, where the marginal Kaplan–Meier estimator is correctly specified, the weighted procedure stays within 0.012 0.012 of nominal across event-free shares, misspecification levels and miscoverage levels. When censoring depends on the covariates, marginal Kaplan–Meier weights fail with the unweighted procedure, at 0.8294 0.8294 in a two-region law where region-stratified weights cover 0.9496 0.9496 , and miss in either direction under a misspecified score, while weights from the true censoring model hold (Section 4.3 ). Table 1 summarises the four cases. 3. A finite-sample coverage floor for the weighted procedure. Lemma 1 establishes weighted exchangeability between the label-complete calibration sample and the test subject, and Theorem 1 gives a floor of 1 − α − Δ w 1-\alpha-\Delta_{w} with Δ w \Delta_{w} explicit in the censoring-model error. The argument is the factorisation of Yi et al. (2025, Appendix A) applied to the selection event { C ≥ min ( T , t ⋆ ) } \{C\geq\min(T,t^{\star})\} in place of { T ≤ C } \{T\leq C\} , with the normalising constant κ \kappa kept explicit and the random size of the complete-case pool accounted for. The cause label changes one step. A hypothesised time determines the test subject’s weight, but a hypothesised cause leaves min ⁡ ( T , t ⋆ ) \min(T,t^{\star}) unknown, so the procedure uses a dominating substitute for that weight, the atom. sections.heading: Related work.
sections.text: Conformal prediction under covariate shift is due to Tibshirani et al. (2019), the penalty for an estimated shift ratio to Lei and Candès (2021), and class-conditional, or Mondrian, conformal prediction to Vovk et al. Podkopaev and Ramdas (2021) reweight conformal classification under label shift. Their weight q ⁡ ( y ) / p ⁡ ( y ) q(y)/p(y) depends on the class index alone, so a hypothesised label determines the test weight, and their calibration set is fully labelled. Our weight 1 / G ⁡ ( min ⁡ ( T , t ⋆ ) ∣ X ) 1/G(\min(T,t^{\star})\mid X) depends on the subject’s event time, which a hypothesised cause leaves unknown. With estimated ratios their statement becomes asymptotic, whereas Theorem 1 keeps a finite-sample floor at an explicit cost Δ w \Delta_{w} . For survival outcomes, the closest in mechanism is Yi et al. (2025), who weight by the inverse probability of censoring with an outcome-dependent weight, and their Theorem 1 is a finite-sample floor minus a censoring-model term. They predict a time and invert a p p -value over candidate values, so the hypothesised object determines the test weight. Shin et al. (2025) add a covariate-shift ratio to this weight for an event-time interval, without a coverage theorem for the combined weight. Candès, Lei and Ren (2023) require Type-I censoring with the censoring time observed on every unit, and the PAC-type guarantees of Gui, Hore, Ren and Barber (2024) do not apply under loss to follow-up. Davidov et al. (2025) extend double robustness to general right censoring with a finite-sample bound whose slack in the weight-estimation error is of the same kind as ours; their bound is a lower bound on a single survival time, holds with probability 1 − δ 1-\delta over the calibration data rather than marginally, and does not treat a cause. Sesia and Svetnik (2025a) handle general right censoring by imputation, and Farina et al. (2026), Qin et al. (2025) and Si and Qiu (2025) give asymptotic guarantees. Holmes and Marandon (2025) give a finite-sample two-sided interval on the subjects that a trained classifier assigns to the uncensored population. Alberge et al. (2025), Wang et al. (2026) and Dang et al. (2026) address the cause or the fold restriction with, respectively, a point prediction, an asymptotic interval, and a finite-sample statement that assumes the exchangeability at issue. Sesia and Svetnik (2025b, 2026) form conformal p p -values from inverse-probability-of-censoring weights on uncensored subjects, for survival thresholds and for selecting patients event-free past a horizon, with asymptotic false discovery rate control and a finite-sample version whose slack is of order n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} (2025b, Theorem 5). For missing and coarsened outcomes, Paul et al. (2025) calibrate a prediction set for a real outcome from monotonely coarsened data through the efficient influence function, with finite-sample validity when some nuisance functions are known. Their threshold takes an infimum over the data consistent with the test covariates, which is the nearest precedent for the atom of ( 3 ). Yin, Shi, Wang and Blei (2024) and Jin, Ren and Candès (2023) give the test slot the upper bound of a response-dependent likelihood ratio, and Yi, Zhang, Tang and Wang (in press) keep a finite-sample floor under nonignorable missingness with a response-dependent propensity. In both, a hypothesised response determines its weight. Fan et al. (2025) keep finite-sample coverage under missing covariates with a response-dependent likelihood ratio, but the response is always observed. A conservative finite-sample guarantee for a set of causes follows by set inclusion from the partial-label construction of Javanmardi et al. (2023, Theorem 1), which calibrates on each subject’s largest score over the labels consistent with its data; a subject censored before the horizon is consistent with every label and enters calibration at its largest score. Liu, de Paula and Tamer (2025) follow a related conservative route for interval-valued outcomes. The guarantee here calibrates on the label-complete subjects and pays only for the censoring-model error.

sections.heading: A common misspecification.
sections.text: A standard competing-risks error acts in the same direction as b b . Estimating each cause’s incidence as one minus a cause-specific survival curve treats the competing event as censoring and understates the event-free probability. We ran this error in all three families over 48 designs at 100 replications each, taking each cause’s curve as one minus the exponential of the negative of the forest’s cause-specific Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard and the event-free probability as one minus their sum, clipped and renormalised (Table 21 ). The equivalent b b reaches 0.1764 0.1764 under exponential hazards, 0.2464 0.2464 under Weibull and 0.3088 0.3088 under non-proportional hazards. These designs use per-draw normalisation and, for Weibull and non-proportional hazards, a censoring rate set from each draw (Appendix C ). The unweighted procedure falls at least two standard errors below nominal in 7 designs, all Weibull or non-proportional at censoring 0.20 0.20 to 0.55 0.55 , and at least four standard errors below in 4, at censoring 0.20 0.20 to 0.40 0.40 . The lowest coverage is 0.8920 0.8920 , under non-proportional hazards at censoring 0.40 0.40 and competing fraction 0.6 0.6 . In a paired comparison on the exponential family (Table 20 ) the weighted procedure does not move with the error, at t t between − 1.1 -1.1 and + 0.9 +0.9 in all 8 cells, while the unweighted procedure falls significantly in 7 of them and stays above nominal. Whether this error alone breaks unweighted calibration depends on the hazard shape rather than on the size of the error.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and limitations
sections.text: In the studied simulation families, a correct outcome model does not protect the unweighted procedure. At the true score it under-covers when few subjects are event-free at the horizon, and under covariate-dependent censoring it can fail badly. A fit that understates the event-free probability lowers coverage at any censoring rate, and whether the total crosses nominal depends jointly on the share, the size of the error, the censoring rate and the hazard shape. In these designs, weights from a correct censoring model kept the weighted procedure near nominal across all of these, and it is the only one of the two procedures with a guarantee, conditional on G ^ \widehat{G} . With a misspecified censoring model it fails with the unweighted procedure, and marginal Kaplan–Meier weights fall below nominal in 4 of the 6 covariate-dependent designs of Table 8 . In these synthetic and semi-synthetic designs the practical question is whether the censoring can be modelled, not whether the outcome model is good. On SEER at t ⋆ = 107 t^{\star}=107 months, the one real censoring mechanism studied, correcting the censoring model changed pooled coverage by 0.0011 0.0011 , and the marginal model was closer to nominal (Section D ). The cells of Table 1 come from different designs. Section 4.2 uses a fitted forest and covariate-free censoring, and Section 4.3 the true score and covariate-dependent censoring, so their magnitudes are not comparable. The synthetic designs outside Section 4.3 share one structure: independent Gaussian covariates, a cause-1 signal on the first covariate and covariate-free exponential censoring, with three hazard families. The real-covariate design of Table 11 departs from it, but its event times are exponential and its censoring synthetic. The bound on Δ w \Delta_{w} is a total-variation coupling with a g min − 2 g_{\min}^{-2} constant. It exceeds α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 in every design we run, while the measured Δ w \Delta_{w} ranges from 0.0035 0.0035 to 0.2371 0.2371 , so it establishes the parametric rate in ∥ G ^ − G ∥ \lVert\widehat{G}-G\rVert but gives no usable number. The penalty is a population quantity in the unknown G G and cannot be estimated from the data. The shrinkage b b is applied to the fitted model’s output rather than obtained by fitting a different model, and at b = 0.6 b=0.6 it understates the event-free rate by a factor of 2.5 2.5 in the cell that crosses. The competing-risks error of Section 4.2 reaches the crossing without shrinkage, under two of the three hazard families. Fitted-score experiments use a competing-risks forest, except Table 16 , and oracle-score experiments use the known class probabilities. Standard errors on the public cohorts are over splits of one fixed sample, so those rows describe the procedure on those cohorts.

sections.heading: Reading Lemma 1 ’s weight functions.
sections.text: The weight functions ( 1 , … , 1 , w ⋆ ) (1,\dots,1,w^{\star}) are the hypothesis of Tibshirani et al.’s Definition 1, not the assignment probabilities they produce. Under their Lemma 3 the case ( 1 , … , 1 , w ) (1,\dots,1,w) collapses to mass proportional to w w on every slot, which is what ( 5 ) states. The two displays sit one sentence apart in that lemma and are not two claims about the same object. Ties. Scores can tie, for instance when the fitted probabilities are constant on groups of covariates. The implementation does not randomise them. It sorts stably and takes the first score whose cumulative weight reaches the target, so tied calibration scores all enter at that point. This is not an assumption of anything proved below. The quantile in ( 2 ) is an infimum, so an inclusive convention can only enlarge the set, and every statement in this paper is a coverage floor. Randomisation would be needed for a matching upper bound, which is not claimed. Remark A2 (Where the weight sits) . Two layers have to be kept apart. At the density layer the assignment computation finds the law of the observed pool proportional to w ⋆ w^{\star} on the test slot and to 1 1 on each calibration slot, and at the procedure layer ( 2 ) is self-normalised, so a common weight on every slot cancels and amounts to asserting plain exchangeability, which holds within ℐ \mathcal{I} and fails against a population test subject whenever w ⋆ w^{\star} is not constant. That is the precise sense in which the unweighted procedure on ℐ \mathcal{I} is a guarantee about a different population rather than no guarantee at all. The sign of its bias depends on the joint law of ( V , w ⋆ ) (V,w^{\star}) , which is what Section 4 varies. The outcome-dependence of w ⋆ w^{\star} is immaterial here, since Definition 1 and the weighted-quantile lemma ask for absolute continuity, not X X -measurability. Remark A3 (The atom need not be constant) . Lemma 2 is stated for any dominating atom, so the sharp choice 1 / G ⁡ ( t ⋆ ∣ X ) 1/G(t^{\star}\mid X) is covered by it directly, and is no larger than 1 / g min 1/g_{\min} . With that atom the mass the calibration fold needs is near the classical 1 / α − 1 1/\alpha-1 rather than g min − 1 g_{\min}^{-1} times it, so the sharp atom is the better one at known G G . No plug-in version of that atom is admissible for this lemma, since under an estimated censoring distribution 1 / G ^ ​ ( t ⋆ ∣ X ) 1/\widehat{G}(t^{\star}\mid X) does not dominate 1 / G ⁡ ( m ∣ X ) 1/G(m\mid X) (Table 4 ). Under the theorem’s estimated weights the plug-in envelope is the right atom (Lemma 3 ).

Cause-of-failure prediction sets under competing risks Sunny Yang guangy4@illinois.edu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Weiyan Zhao Affiliation: Northumbria University Abstract Split conformal prediction sets for competing-risks labels at a fixed horizon require calibration labels that right censoring can leave unobserved. Complete-case calibration guarantees coverage for the label-complete subpopulation, but its population coverage can deviate in either direction, even at the true class probabilities. We study how selection changes the score distribution near the population quantile. At the true score in our main simulation family, with independent draws, complete-case calibration covers 0.8723 at a nominal 0.900 when 22% of subjects are event-free at the horizon. In 4 of 48 further designs using per-draw normalisation, estimating cause incidences as one minus the exponential of the negative of the cause-specific Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazards, with the event-free probability as the clipped and renormalised remainder, puts complete-case coverage at least four standard errors below nominal. In these designs, weights from a correctly specified censoring model keep coverage near nominal. Extending the argument of Yi et al. (2025) to a cause label, we establish a finite-sample coverage lower bound with an explicit penalty for censoring-model error. Misspecifying the censoring model can also lead to under-coverage. 1 Introduction For a competing-risks model, a natural prediction at a fixed horizon is a set of causes, possibly including event-free status, that contains the realised label at the horizon for at least 1 − α 1-\alpha of subjects. Split conformal prediction gives such a set from any fitted model when the calibration labels are observed. Under right censoring they are not, since a subject who leaves follow-up before the horizon without an event has no label. Complete-case calibration keeps the subjects whose label is determined and drops the rest. It selects on the outcome, because a subject who fails early is more likely to have been followed long enough than one who survives past the horizon, and the exchangeability that conformal prediction relies on is lost. Boström et al. (2019) use this procedure for a binary event-by-horizon label and state its guarantee for the subjects not censored before the horizon. Boström et al. (2023) keep the censored subjects, with a Kaplan–Meier estimate within each Mondrian category, to give a predictive distribution for the event time. Reports on the population disagree. Dang et al. (2026) find complete-case conformal under-covering, attribute it to the censoring rate and recommend a switch above 40%. Farina et al. (2026) find their complete-case comparator over-covering in every setting they run, but their target is a lower prediction bound on the event time, for which selection toward short observed times is conservative by construction. Neither account applies to a label at a horizon. We characterise when complete-case calibration is safe for a cause-of-failure label and when weighting the calibration sample by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored repairs it. The paper makes three contributions. 1. The complete-case error can take either sign, even at the true score. Complete-case calibration takes its threshold from the score distribution of the selected subjects, and we study how this selection changes coverage over the population. At fixed covariates, subjects event-free at the horizon have the lowest selection probability, so the event-free share, error in the fitted event-free probability and the dependence of censoring on the covariates all shift the selected score distribution relative to the population’s. The direction of the mean score shift indicates the sign of the error but does not determine it (Appendix F ). In our main simulation family at the true score, the unweighted procedure over-covers at an event-free share of 0.544 0.544 and under-covers at 0.224 0.224 , where it covers 0.8723 0.8723 at a nominal 0.900 0.900 over 200 200 replications with independent draws (Section 4.1 ). In a two-region law where most subjects are event-free, the true score still under-covers (Section 4.3 ). A fit that understates the event-free probability lowers coverage, censoring amplifies both effects, and the observed crossing point moves with the censoring rate, so no threshold on the censoring rate locates the failure. Estimating each cause’s incidence as one minus a cause-specific survival curve, with the event-free probability as the remainder, puts the unweighted procedure at least four standard errors below nominal in 4 of 48 designs (Section 4.2 ). 2.
